cultivar: Jingshan local landrace, Jiukeng and Longjing 43
processing: Baked green: tender shoots are fired, lightly rolled to a loose curl and dried with warm air, keeping the down and a fresh, delicate aroma.
harvest_season: Spring, late March to late April; pre-Qingming and yu qian lots of a bud with one or two leaves.
appearance_dry: Fine, loosely curled shoots, bright green with abundant white down.
appearance_liquor: Pale, bright green-gold with a faint haze of down.
appearance_wet: Small, tender bud-and-leaf sets, uniformly bright green.
taste_profile: Fresh and sweet with orchid and young chestnut, a soft umami body and a clean, cool finish; delicate but not thin.

brewing.notes: Glass or gaiwan at 80 °C. Water first, then leaf, as for any downy tea; three steeps, and the first is the fragrant one.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest from the Jingshan hills, graded by picking date (pre-Qingming, yu qian) and by bud ratio; mostly sold within Zhejiang and through Hangzhou shops. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Jingshan tea comes from the hills around Jingshan Temple in Yuhang, on the northern edge of Hangzhou, a Zen monastery whose Song-dynasty tea gatherings are credited in both Chinese and Japanese accounts with shaping the Japanese tea ceremony: Japanese monks studied here and took the tea rituals home. The tea itself is a modern revival of that monastic tradition, a downy baked green.

It is a soft style: fired, barely rolled, dried gently with warm air, so the fine shoots keep their silver down and a fresh, floral aroma. The look is close to a small Mao Feng; the feel in the cup is lighter and cooler.

It drinks fresh and sweet, orchid over young chestnut, with a soft savoury body and a clean finish. Three steeps at 80 °C in a glass is its format, and it is one of the better greens to drink slightly cooler, around 75 °C, where the sweetness comes forward. Overheated it goes grassy quickly.

It is sold as the spring crop of the current year, graded by picking date, and most of it is drunk in Hangzhou, where it is a respected local alternative to Longjing. The temple connection generates a lot of ceremonial packaging; buy the tea, not the box. Look for even, downy shoots with a sweet smell and a picking date in late March or April.

If you are in Hangzhou in April, a half-day at Jingshan with a glass of the fresh tea is a better use of time than the West Lake crowds.
sources_note: No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. The Japanese-tea-ceremony link is the traditional account; revival date 'late 1970s' follows Chinese sources.
history:
Jingshan's reputation comes from its temple. Tea is said to have been grown here since the monastery's Tang founding, and the tradition that Lu Yu lived on the mountain while writing is repeated locally. The temple peaked in the Song, when its tea rituals became a model for Chan houses.

Japanese temple tea ceremonies trace themselves to Jingshan, and an eighteenth-century Japanese reference work credits the monk Nanpo Shomyo with carrying the ritual home after studying here around 1259. The modern phrase 'Jingshan tea banquet' is much younger: it took shape through exchanges with Japan from the 1980s, and the ritual was reconstructed in 2008.

The tea in the cup today is a modern green built on that old name. Its monastic tradition faded from the Ming onward.
